title: In 22 western US burned areas, postfire debris flows needed about 2.2 times higher 15-minute rain intensity after the first postfire year, and USGS M1 over-predicted more in years 2-3
abstract: Question: in the same burned areas, does the rainfall intensity that is necessary for a runoff-generated debris flow increase with time since fire, and does the USGS M1 likelihood model stay calibrated after the first year? Data: the USGS runoff-generated postfire debris-flow inventory v1 (Graber et al. 2026, CC0; 8,981 records, 80 fires, 2000-2025). Method: a plan written before model fits; a logistic model with one intercept for each fire, ln(peak 15-minute intensity I15) and a term for postfire years 2-4, on the 22 fires with records in year 1 and later (4,858 records, 746 storms, 339 debris flows). Findings: debris flows needed 2.21 times higher I15 after the first year (fire bootstrap 95% interval 1.67 to 3.06; within-fire storm-label permutation p = 0.0002; leave-one-fire-out 2.07 to 2.34). The threshold did not change measurably inside year 1 (factor 1.04 per doubling of days, 0.91 to 1.19) and was 2.7 to 2.8 times higher at 366-1,095 days. Storm-level, same-segment, systematic-segment, season, rainfall-ratio and M1-watershed-term checks gave factors of 2.0 to 3.5. M1 over-predicted debris flows in all years: observed/expected was 0.42 in year 1, 0.25 in year 2 and 0.075 in year 3 (all fires); at the 22 panel fires it fell from 0.37 to 0.10. Year 4 is not resolved (few records, probable reporting of debris flows only). Limitations: a compiled, not complete, sample with possible changes in observation effort; 22 fires; gauge-to-watershed distance; infiltration recovery and sediment exhaustion cannot be separated.
